power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

"National EIR simulated by VECTRI in the future. (a) Mean monthly EIR for 1995-2014 (with 10th-472 90th percentiles of years) and for the four scenario-periods; shading: SMC window (July-October). (b) National 473 changes in annual EIR, detectable parasite ratio and share of the EIR in July-October; *: Mann-Whitney p < 0.05.", 
"Suitability: rule-based season (16-34 °C, ≥ 60 mm), median 477 of ten models and number of models with a significant change (Mann-Whitney p < 0.05).",

text.text: Background.

Malaria transmission in Senegal is seasonal and spatially heterogeneous, but the consistency of dynamical malaria models with routine surveillance has rarely been tested with monthly subnational data.

We analysed monthly confirmed cases from the National Malaria Control Programme (PNLP) regional database (14 regions, 2009-2025)  and reports of the 79 health districts (2016)(2017)(2018)(2019)(2020)(2021)(2022)(2023)(2024)(2025).

Ten bias-adjusted NEX-GDDP-CMIP6 models (1995-2014; SSP2-4.5    and SSP5-8.5 to 2100) were evaluated against CHIRPS rainfall; VECTRI was driven by MRI-ESM2-0, the model closest to the ensemble median change.

text.text: Results.
National incidence averaged 24.5 cases per 1,000 per year without trend over 2009-2024, but increased in Kédougou, Kolda and Tambacounda, which reported 58.7 % of cases for 11.3 % of the population.
The test positivity rate (TPR) decreased from 22.5 % in 2016 to 16.2 % in 2024.

Based on the seasonal centre of gravity, observed cases lagged the entomological inoculation rate (EIR) simulated by VECTRI by 1.06 months (95 % CI 0.88-1.23) and the lag was positive in 13 of 14 regions, but the regional differences in timing were not reproduced.
Across 45 departments, the simulated EIR was correlated with the TPR (Spearman ρ = 0.67, 95 % CI 0.47-0.79).
In 2025, confirmed cases decreased by 55.7 % in the 34 districts of the longlasting insecticidal net (LLIN) mass campaign against 9.7 % elsewhere.

text.text: Conclusions.
VECTRI driven by bias-adjusted CMIP6 climate reproduces the timing of the malaria season and the gradient of transmission intensity in Senegal, but not the regional differences in timing.
The TPR is a population-free indicator for model evaluation.
Seasonal malaria chemoprevention calendars should account for the regional timing documented here; the projected changes in timing are small.

text.text: Two limitations recur in these studies.

First, their evaluation against observed malaria has relied on short periods, sentinel sites or annual totals [2, 20], whereas the National Malaria Control Programme (PNLP) now reports monthly data for all health districts, including the number of suspected and tested patients, which allows the test positivity rate (TPR) to be computed [23].

text.text: This study has four objectives: (i) to describe the seasonality, spatial distribution, trends and severity of confirmed malaria in Senegal from the PNLP regional database (2009-2025) and harmonised district reports (2016-2025); (ii) to evaluate the bias-adjusted CMIP6 rainfall against observations and the timing and spatial pattern of transmission simulated by VECTRI against surveillance data, at the national, regional and departmental scales; (iii) to describe the 2025 surveillance data in relation to the LLIN mass distribution campaign; and (iv) to project changes in climatic suitability and simulated transmission under two emission scenarios.
Senegal (about 197,000 km 2 ) is divided into 14 regions and 45 departments (GADM version 4.1 boundaries, https://gadm.org) and into 79 health districts.

The analysis is conducted on a regular 0.25° grid (331 cells overlapping Senegal), with the share of each cell inside each region and department used as aggregation weight together with the cell area.

text.text: The regional database provides monthly confirmed malaria cases (rapid diagnostic test or microscopy) and malaria deaths for the 14 regions from 2008 to 2025, with the regional population of the National Agency of Statistics and Demography (ANSD).
The year 2008 was excluded because of the change of regional boundaries, and 2025 is provisional; the analysis period is 2009-2024 (16 years), and 2025 is reported separately.
The district reports were harmonised from the annual Excel reports of 2016-2020 and the District Health Information Software 2 (DHIS2) exports of 2021-2025.

They provide, by district and month, the number of suspected, tested and confirmed outpatient cases for children under five years, patients aged five years and over (excluding pregnant women) and pregnant women, the number of hospitalised malaria cases (hospitalised severe malaria in 2016-2019, hospitalised confirmed malaria from 2020) and malaria deaths, and, for 2021-2025, the number of LLINs distributed through routine channels.

In the 2016-2019 reports, 36 to 37 hospitals were reported as separate units; they were added to the district in which they are located, as in the 2020 report and the DHIS2 exports, which integrate hospitals in their district.

Districts created after 2016 (Sangalkam, Yeumbeul and Diakhao) have no separate report before their creation; analyses over 2016-2025 were therefore made by department (GADM level 2, each district being assigned to the department where it lies) or by region.
All reporting-unit names were matched.
The district reports also provide the number of LLINs distributed during the 2025 mass distribution campaign (CDM) in 34 districts.

In the DHIS2 exports, 235 of the 3,792 district-months of 2021-2024 (6.2 %) had no value for confirmed cases although the number of tested patients was reported (mean 720 tests); 94.5 % of them fell between January and June, mostly in low-transmission districts of Louga, Fatick and Matam.
Because DHIS2 does not store zero values, they were counted as zero.
Monthly report completeness, available for 2017-2020, ranged from 95.7 % to 99.6 %.

Annual national totals of the two sources were identical for 2016-2020 and differed by -0.2 % (2021), +0.0 % (2023) and -0.1 % (2024); in 2022, the regional database was 21.8 % lower (358,033 against 458,040 confirmed cases), with lower values in all regions (S1 Fig).

The regional database is used for the long period and the district reports for testing, positivity, age, severity and departmental analyses; the sensitivity of the main result to 2022 and to the source was assessed.

text.text: The correlation between the simulated and observed mean seasonal cycles was at least 0.99 for all models, and the rainfall centre of gravity differed from CHIRPS by 0.02 to 0.19 month nationally (MRI-ESM2-0: +0.07 month, about two days).

Regionally, the bias of MRI-ESM2-0 ranged from +1 % (Ziguinchor) and +4 % (Kédougou) to +27 % (Kaolack, Dakar) and +29 % (Kaffrine), and the timing difference from -0.10 (Dakar) to +0.14 month (Saint-Louis).
The forcing therefore reproduces the timing of the rainy season, with a wet bias of 10-30 % relative to CHIRPS in the centre and west.

Transmission simulated by VECTRI Driven by MRI-ESM2-0, VECTRI simulated a national mean annual EIR of 404 infective bites per person per year (10th-90th percentiles of years 312-518) over 1995-2014, with a single wave: 20.6 bites per person in July, 85.3 in August, 151.4 in September, 106.6 in October and 29.4 in November (Fig 7; S5 Fig).

The EIR peaked in September in 16 of the 20 years and in October in four years; its centre of gravity was 9.08 (95 % CI 8.98-9.20), the concentration R was 0.85, 75 % of the annual EIR occurred within three months, and 90.7 % between July and October.

The EIR exceeded 500 bites per person per year in Kolda (707), Sédhiou (656), Kédougou (583) and Tambacounda (520), and was low in Thiès (44) and negligible in Dakar (0.3), where the high population density reduces the number of bites per person in VECTRI (Fig 7a).
The longest run of months with EIR ≥ 1 averaged 7.9 months, with the longest seasons in the centre and south-west (Fig 7b).

The simulated timing varied little in space (centre of gravity 8.95-9.78 across departments; Fig 7c), and the detectable parasite ratio averaged 72 % (Fig 7d), a level that reflects the absence of calibration and of interventions in the simulations rather than the current prevalence.

480 481 Principal findings 482 This study combines sixteen years of monthly regional surveillance, nine years of harmonised 483 district reports with testing data, observed rainfall, ten bias-adjusted CMIP6 models and 484 VECTRI simulations to evaluate the description of malaria seasonality in Senegal by a 485 dynamical model and to project its changes.
text.formatted: <head>480</head> 481 Principal findings 482 This study combines sixteen years of monthly regional surveillance, nine years of harmonised 483 district reports with testing data, observed rainfall, ten bias-adjusted CMIP6 models and 484 VECTRI simulations to evaluate the description of malaria seasonality in Senegal by a 485 dynamical model and to project its changes.

text.text: Four results stand out.

First, the timing of 486 confirmed malaria is regular, centred on mid-October, and reported cases lag the transmission 487 simulated by VECTRI by about one month nationally and in 13 of 14 regions and 44 of 45 488 departments; this lag is robust to the observation period and source.

Second, the delay between 489 rainfall and reported cases (about two months) is shared equally between the delay between 490 rainfall and transmission, which VECTRI reproduces with a nearly uniform value of one month, 491 and the delay between transmission and recorded cases; the regional differences in observed 492 timing arise in the second part and are not reproduced by the model.
Third, the simulated EIR reproduces the spatial gradient of transmission intensity measured by the TPR, whereas the simulated cases do not reproduce the distribution of the burden.

Fourth, the projected changes in timing are small, while the intensity of transmission is projected to decrease strongly only under SSP5-8.5 at the end of the century, with increases in the south-east under the other scenarios.

The one-month lag between simulated transmission and confirmed cases is consistent with previous modelling studies in Senegal, which placed the transmission peak in September-October and reported cases one to two months after the rainfall peak [2, 3, 13], and with entomological and epidemiological observations in the Sahel, where vector abundance precedes clinical malaria by several weeks [42].
text.formatted: The one-month lag between simulated transmission and confirmed cases is consistent with previous modelling studies in Senegal, which placed the transmission peak in September-October and reported cases one to two months after the rainfall peak <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">[2,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">3,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">13]</ref>, and with entomological and epidemiological observations in the Sahel, where vector abundance precedes clinical malaria by several weeks <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">[42]</ref>.

text.text: It is compatible with an intrinsic incubation period of the order of two weeks for Plasmodium falciparum and with the delays of care seeking, diagnosis and reporting.
Hospitalised cases followed outpatient cases by about one week, as expected for the progression to severe disease.

With three quarters of annual cases within four consecutive months, malaria in Senegal meets the criterion of marked seasonality proposed by Roca-Feltrer et al. [43], which underlies eligibility for SMC [44].
text.formatted: With three quarters of annual cases within four consecutive months, malaria in Senegal meets the criterion of marked seasonality proposed by Roca-Feltrer et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">[43]</ref>, which underlies eligibility for SMC <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">[44]</ref>.

text.text: The separation of the delay into two parts of about one month each is, to our knowledge, new for Senegal.

It was made possible because the bias-adjusted forcing reproduces the timing of observed rainfall to within a few days, so that the simulated delay between rainfall and transmission can be compared with the observed delay between rainfall and cases.
The uniformity of the simulated delay across regions contrasts with observed delays ranging from 1.3 months in Kédougou to 2.8 months in Sédhiou.
Three types of factors not represented in VECTRI may explain this contrast.

Hydrology: in Casamance and in the centre-west (Kaolack, Fatick, Diourbel), flooded areas, rice fields, the Saloum and Casamance estuaries and other persistent water bodies can maintain breeding sites after the end of the rains, as shown by pondresolving hydrological modelling [11, 42, 45], which would extend transmission into November-December.
text.formatted: Hydrology: in Casamance and in the centre-west (Kaolack, Fatick, Diourbel), flooded areas, rice fields, the Saloum and Casamance estuaries and other persistent water bodies can maintain breeding sites after the end of the rains, as shown by pondresolving hydrological modelling <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">[11,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">42,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">45]</ref>, which would extend transmission into November-December.

text.text: Interventions: SMC delivered from July to October [6, 46] reduces cases among children during the rounds and may shift the remaining cases later; the decrease of the share of children under five among confirmed cases over the period is consistent with this effect, but the data do not allow it to be quantified.
text.formatted: Interventions: SMC delivered from July to October <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">[6,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">46]</ref> reduces cases among children during the rounds and may shift the remaining cases later; the decrease of the share of children under five among confirmed cases over the period is consistent with this effect, but the data do not allow it to be quantified.

text.text: Reporting and care seeking may also differ between regions.

Conversely, the early season in Kédougou, where cases nearly coincide with simulated transmission, coincides with the earliest and most abundant rainfall and the highest burden, and suggests that the early part of the season is underestimated by the model in the south-east, where the season has also become later between 2009-2014 and 2015-2024.
The TPR is well suited to evaluate dynamical malaria models with routine data.
Because almost all suspected cases were tested, it measures the share of febrile patients with a malaria infection and does not depend on population estimates, which are uncertain at fine scale.

Across departments, the simulated EIR was slightly more strongly correlated with the TPR than observed rainfall, although the confidence intervals overlap; the combination of rainfall, temperature and population represented by VECTRI therefore reproduces the gradient at least as well as rainfall alone.

The concentration of the burden in Kédougou, Kolda and Tambacounda, where incidence increased over 2009-2024, is consistent with the persistent south-eastern hotspots identified over 2000-2020 [47] and with the gradient of simulated transmission [3, 4, 19, 20].

text.text: The simulated case counts should therefore not be used to allocate resources between regions without calibration.

The higher share of children under five where the TPR is high, and the lower ratio of deaths to confirmed cases in high-transmission regions, are consistent with the age shift of clinical malaria with transmission intensity [48] and with the relation between transmission intensity and the clinical spectrum of severe malaria [49].

text.text: The high ratios in Saint-Louis, Dakar and Thiès may also reflect the referral of severe patients to regional and national hospitals and the lower immunity of populations with little exposure; patient-level data would be needed to distinguish these explanations.

National incidence showed no trend over 2009-2024, but the TPR decreased significantly over 2016-2024 while testing remained near universal, and incidence increased in the south-east and decreased in the centre and west.

A decreasing TPR with a stable number of confirmed cases indicates that more patients with non-malarial fevers were tested (1.56 million suspected cases in 2016, 2.91 million in 2024); national incidence alone would therefore hide both a change in testing practice and a geographical concentration of transmission.

In 2025, confirmed cases decreased by more than half in the districts of the LLIN mass campaign, against less than 10 % elsewhere, with a stable number of tests in these districts and a decrease that started in July, after the first half of the year was close to the usual level.
This pattern is consistent with an effect of the campaign on transmission, in line with the large contribution of insecticide-treated nets to the decrease of malaria in Africa [50].
text.formatted: This pattern is consistent with an effect of the campaign on transmission, in line with the large contribution of insecticide-treated nets to the decrease of malaria in Africa <ref type="bibr">[50]</ref>.

text.text: It cannot, however, be attributed to the campaign from these data: the campaign districts were selected for their high burden, the 2025 data are provisional, the number of tests also decreased in October-December in the campaign districts, Kolda was flagged as possibly incomplete, and the decrease of confirmed cases in November in the other districts suggests incomplete late-year reporting.
A verification of the 2025 data with the PNLP and a comparison with SMC coverage and rainfall will be needed.

The ten models agree on warming but not on the sign of rainfall change, a known feature of CMIP projections over the Sahel [51]; the median decrease of annual rainfall concerns the core of the rainy season, while October rainfall increases slightly.

Driving VECTRI with the model closest to the ensemble median keeps the projected malaria changes representative of the central climate change, but does not describe their spread; the rule-based approach, driven by all ten models, provides this spread for suitability.

Both approaches agree that the changes are small by mid-century and under SSP2-4.5, and that transmission decreases under SSP5-8.5 at the end of the century, when temperatures exceed the thermal optimum for transmission [22] during more months and rainfall decreases by about one third.

text.text: They also agree on a smaller decrease, or an increase, in the south-east, where the burden is concentrated.

For SMC, the main projection result is the stability of the seasonal timing: the centre of gravity of simulated transmission moves by less than 0.1 month and the share of the annual EIR in July-October remains about 90 % in all scenarios.

The present calendar would therefore remain aligned with the climatic window of transmission, and the regional differences in observed timing, of more than one month between Kédougou and Casamance or the centre-west, matter more for planning than the projected changes.

A regionally differentiated SMC calendar, starting earlier in the south-east and extending to November in the regions with late seasons, would be consistent with these results and with the protection decay observed after each round in Kédougou [46].

text.text: The strengths of this study are the use of two independent surveillance sources with nearuniversal testing, the harmonisation of district reports across formats, the evaluation of the climate forcing against observations, the use of ten bias-adjusted models and of an objective criterion to select the model driving VECTRI, the decomposition of the delay between rainfall and cases, and the use of resampling statistics without pairing simulated and observed years.
Several limitations must be considered.

CMIP6 historical simulations do not reproduce the observed chronology of years, so the comparison is restricted to climatological seasonality and spatial patterns and cannot assess interannual skill; driving VECTRI with observed or reanalysis forcing over the surveillance period would allow this evaluation.

VECTRI was driven by a single model, and its parameters were not calibrated; the absolute EIR, the parasite ratio and the simulated cases are not realistic for current conditions, which include interventions, and the projections assume that interventions remain absent.
The 0.25° grid represents Dakar by few cells, and the population is interpolated from 1°.
Bias-adjusted rainfall is 10-30 % wetter than CHIRPS in the centre and west, which may lengthen the simulated season there.
The two observed sources differ in 2022, although the main result did not depend on this year, and 2025 data are provisional.
The comparison of departments relies on the assignment of districts to departments, whose boundaries differ.
Finally, SMC coverage, indoor residual spraying and case management were not available by month and district and were not analysed.
Confirmed malaria in Senegal follows a regular seasonal cycle centred on mid-October, with a burden increasingly concentrated in the south-east.

VECTRI driven by bias-adjusted CMIP6 climate reproduces the timing of transmission and its spatial gradient: reported cases lag simulated transmission by about one month, and simulated transmission lags rainfall by about one month.
The model does not reproduce the regional differences in timing or the distribution of clinical cases, which depend on hydrology, immunity, population and the health system.

Seasonality of testing, confirmed cases and severe malariaNationally, the peak of confirmed cases occurred in October in 10 of the 16 years of 2009-2024, in November in five years and in September in one year.

The seasonal centre of gravity was 10.14 (95 % CI 10.00-10.27), between 9.40 (2022) and 10.52 (2015), with a concentration R of 0.68; 75 % of annual cases occurred within four consecutive months (median over years), and 75.3 % (95 % CI 71.9-78.6 %) occurred between August and November (S4 Fig).

The seasonality of confirmed cases was not driven by testing (Fig4a): over 2016-2024, the number of tested patients varied only 4.8-fold between the lowest and the highest month of the mean cycle (R = 0.36) against 67-fold for confirmed cases (R = 0.69), and the TPR rose from 2.0 % in May to 33.6 % in November (Fig4b).

Hospitalised cases followed outpatient confirmed cases by 0.21 month (95 % CI 0.04 to 0.38; centre of gravity 10.28), and malaria deaths had the same timing as confirmed cases (10.19; difference 0.12 month, -0.10 to 0.33).

The projected timing of transmission is stable under all scenarios, while its intensity decreases strongly only under SSP5-8.5 at the end of the century.

Driving VECTRI with observed forcing, calibrating it against the TPR, including interventions and verifying the 2025 data are the next steps towards climate-informed planning of SMC and early warning.
